newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE -- Colombia's Coffee Fund running on empty.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE -- Colombia's Coffee Fund running on empty.

text.p: Colombia's National Coffee Fund, an institution credited with bringing jealously-guarded stability to the country's coffee industry for decades, faces a deepening financial crisis that could force sweeping changes in the industry.
Jorge Cardenas, veteran leader of the National Coffee Growers' Federation, said this week that the fund was basically going bust and that it will have to undergo radical changes if it is to survive.

At that point, "the fund will have exhausted its liquidity both at home and abroad," Cardenas said. "All of its debt capacity will have been committed and it won't have the resources to be able to purchase the crop."

The fund, which guarantees the purchase of all Colombian coffee, has paid growers support prices for years. It it were to stop buying coffee it could open the industry up to unbridled laws of supply and demand, leaving growers to negotiate directly with private exporters.

The fund -- jointly administered by the government and National Coffee Growers' Federation -- finances public works projects in Colombia's central coffee-growing areas and bankrolls scientific investigation, along with an ongoing fight against the plague known as "broca" that has infected more than half of Colombia's coffee plantations.
It also pays for the successful advertising campaign that has turned Juan Valdez and "100 percent Colombian" into trademark recognized around the world.

Although it co-owns the fund, the central government is legally barred from bailing it out by writing off its debts. It also has little or no control over monetary and exchange rate policy, which is dictated by the central bank. Apart from rising oil income, the bank blames much of the peso's rise on the government's growing dependence on foreign credits to finance its fiscal deficit at home.

In remarks to reporters on the sidelines of the annual meeting in Bogota Tuesday, Cardenas strongly hinted that the Coffee Fund will be scaling back on some of its activities, or dropping them altogether, in an effort to get its economic house in order.
"It's a very complex situation," he said of the fund's finances. "It can't continue doing everything that it's been doing. It has to reform."
Some private coffee exporters said this week that they would welcome the fund's outright collapse since it could open up Colombia's tightly-regulated market to free competition.

Others noted this could jeopardize the coffee industry's role as the single largest source of employment in Colombia, however, since many small and mid-sized growers would be forced out of business without support prices.

And the relative peace of the central coffee-growing region -- an area where guerrilla violence has been kept at bay through the fund's financing of everything from schools and clinics to roads and sports centers -- could also vanish with the fund.
"It would be traumatic to say the least," one trader said.
